Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Baltimore MD/Washington DC
330 PM EDT Wed Aug 12 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
Have raised chances for showers this evening as a decaying line
potentially tracks across the area. However, confidence does
remain on the lower side given all of the thick high clouds
overhead. Otherwise, the forecast largely remains on track.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
- 1) Decreasing storm coverage today before ramping up late in
  the week with a returning warm front.

- 2) Showers and thunderstorms possible between Sunday and
  Monday before becoming drier into early next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Decreasing storm coverage today before ramping
up late in the week with a returning warm front.

The earlier frontal boundary has now settled down near the
Virginia-North Carolina border. To the north, temperatures are
holding steady in the low/mid 80s with mainly 60s dew points.
With diurnal heating, some shallow cumulus fields have formed,
but these are largely capped by the limited instability.
Otherwise, filtered sunshine is noted amidst passing high clouds
and elevated smoke from the western U.S. wildfires. 

Upstream convection which continues to train over eastern
Indiana/western Ohio should stay well west of the local area.
Convective activity is likely to follow the instability gradient
which ushers this convection into eastern Kentucky. Aside from
this complex, a few high-resolution solutions attempt to form
some cells across the Lower Great Lakes. This would carry
isolated showers and embedded thunderstorms toward the Mason-
Dixon Line by the mid/late evening. While not severe, these
could carry a risk of brief heavy rainfall and lightning. Any
such activity exits toward the Eastern Shore after around 2 AM.
Some patchy fog may form west of the Blue Ridge, accompanied by
area-wide lows in the 60s, with low 70s along/east of I-95.

Heights further build on Thursday into Friday as upper ridging
stretches up from the Gulf of America into the central and
southeastern U.S. Locally, being north of this ridge will favor
continued northwesterly flow aloft which carries the risk of
mesoscale convective systems (MCS) intrusions. On Thursday, the
main shower and thunderstorm chances focus across the
Alleghenies down into the central Virginia Piedmont and I-64
corridor. This largely ties to the front still being displaced
off toward the south. Eventual northward progression is possible
into Friday which introduces a better chance for storms. The
latest ensembles support probabilities in the 40 to 70 percent
range. While not a washout by any means, this should be heavily
guided by the peak in daytime heating. High temperatures each
day will be in the 80s to low 90s, with 70s for the mountains.
Likewise, seasonable conditions can be expected overnight.

Ample high pressure builds to the north of the region on 
Saturday as the frontal zone again sags back toward the 
Carolinas. An onshore component to the wind could keep some
additional cloud cover around. However, overall trends suggest a
drop off in humidity before winds return to southerly late in
the weekend.


KEY MESSAGE 2... Showers and thunderstorms possible between
Sunday and Monday before becoming drier into early next week.

Upper-level ridging continues to build over the Southwest CONUS over 
the weekend, with multiple shortwave troughs tracking to the east 
offshore of New England. Beginning Sunday, an upper-level 
perturbation forms over the Canadian Rockies and tracks eastward, 
with a stemming frontal boundary tracking across the East Coast late 
Sunday and into Monday. This boundary will likely bring chances for 
scattered showers and thunderstorms here in the Mid-Atlantic, 
although model guidance has been somewhat marginal on the severe 
potential for this event. As of the 12z ensemble runs, several 
outputs have the highest likelihood for severe weather just south of 
the area towards southern VA and the Carolinas, while the GFS 
ensemble runs still have a 15%-30% probability for severe weather 
centered within the region. Should any thunderstorms become severe, 
the most likely hazards will likely be elevated wind gusts as well 
as locally heavy rainfall. As drought conditions continue to improve 
within the region, flooding potential becomes more of a concern with 
any heavy rainfall-producing thunderstorms that materialize. 

Otherwise, temperatures remain near-normal for mid-August, with 
humid conditions as well as temperatures ranging in the 80s and 
lower-90s at times near the metros. High pressure moves into the 
region once the frontal boundary passes offshore by Tuesday, 
bringing drier conditions to the region.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z WEDNESDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
While VFR conditions are expected into Thursday, have introduced
a PROB30 for thunderstorm restrictions late this evening. 
Otherwise, winds remain somewhat variable and light given
continued weak gradients. Winds on Thursday should be mainly out
of the west to northwest with the frontal zone off to the south.
Any afternoon/evening storms should be confined closer to I-64
around KCHO, with others to the north remaining dry. More
widespread showers and thunderstorms are possible on Friday
which would favor further convective-driven restrictions. High
pressure builds to the north on Saturday which should favor VFR
conditions amidst east to northeasterly winds.

Beginning Sunday, a cold front could bring sub-VFR conditions to 
terminals as scattered showers and thunderstorms are possible 
throughout the region. These conditions could be intermittent 
through Monday as the front passes through. Southeast winds shift 
northwest Monday evening in the wake of the front.

&&

.MARINE...
Background winds remain on the weaker side as a frontal zone
sags off toward the south. Gusts will mostly be in the 5 to 10
knot range, while pushing up to 15 knots at times when southerly
channeling occurs. The main threat for hazardous marine
conditions would be on Friday given more widespread showers and
thunderstorms. Any storm will be capable of gusty winds and
frequent lightning. This front drops toward the Carolinas on
Saturday as high pressure builds over the northeastern U.S. The
resulting winds will mainly be out of the east to northeast.

SCAs will likely be needed by Sunday afternoon as a cold front 
tracks through the region. Between Sunday & Monday, gusty showers 
and thunderstorms are possible over the waters. Winds diminish once 
the front passes through late Monday. Southeast winds shift 
northwest by Monday evening in the wake of the front.

&&

.TIDES/COASTAL FLOODING...
Water levels will slowly elevate in the next couple of days.
This brings a more sensitive location like Annapolis into Action
Stage for the Thursday morning high tide. However, there is
currently no discernible threat for coastal flooding this week.

&&

.LWX WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
DC...None.
MD...None.
VA...None.
WV...None.
MARINE...None.

&&
